SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.

Running SST's `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account.

SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
SST's team began the Ion rewrite in late 2023, replacing SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's documentation ("What is SST") states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis," wrote: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

claims.text: The published `package.json` for SST's platform package lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's architecture, `sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, which compile into Pulumi resource declarations, after which the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations, then Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works the same way (without requiring a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud) for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The same Terraform provider bridge that lets SST use Terraform providers also lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Nitric's own documentation states: "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric's official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers, since SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket rather than Pulumi's hosted service.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code, working entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs/components compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can still be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.

SST's broadened team attention is a legitimate expansion of what the team works on, not a sign that SST is being abandoned, as evidenced by its releases and download numbers.

Since SST v3, `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI, and SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.

SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself, and SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
SST's team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

Pulumi used directly exposes capabilities SST doesn't expose on its own — cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application — since it's the same engine SST already runs on.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Pulumi's policy as code provides guardrails that a platform team can enforce centrally.
Pulumi's components feature enables sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.
